newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan P.M. to meet allies over Okinawa U.S. bases.
newsitem.headline: Japan P.M. to meet allies over Okinawa U.S. bases.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto called an emergency meeting with his parliamentary allies on Thursday to discuss a looming row with the island of Okinawa over the future of U.S. military bases there.

Hashimoto was due to meet Socialist party chairman Takako Doi and Akiko Domoto of the small Sakigake party to discuss possible revision of laws that allow private land to expropriated for U.S. military use.
The laws are at the heart of the central government's festering row with the southern island that has heated up again ahead of the May 15 expiration of leases on plots of land used by U.S. bases.
About 3,000 people own the plots, which cover 362,000 square metres (433,000 sq. yds.) of land on 12 bases including the U.S. Air Force's huge Kadena Air Base.
The law revisions would allow the central government to by-pass lengthy land expropriation procedures by provincial governments.
Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota, who wants all U.S. bases on the island shut by 2015, has warned Hashimoto against rushing the revision, called the Special Land Lease Law, through parliament.
The Socialists oppose the revision and the country's two main opposition parties have not made up their minds.
The Okinawa issue will figure high in a flurry of Japanese diplomatic activity with the United States over the next two months.

American Vice President Al Gore visits Japan from March 23-24 and U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen was also likely to come to Tokyo this month. Hashimoto is scheduled to visit Washington in late April.
Without a revision of the laws, the extension of leases on the plots in question may not be possible beyond May 15, making the occupation of the land illegal.
The issue was a rallying cry among anti-bases campaigners in Okinawa last year, many of whom own plots of land.

The bases controversy erupted in September 1995 after the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, which put the spotlight on the concentration of the U.S. military presence on Okinawa.
Okinawa houses 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan and is home to half of the 40,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in Japan.
Soon after the rape case, for which the servicemen were jailed, Governor Ota launched his anti-bases campaign by rejecting approval of land expropriation for some U.S. bases.
In a rare battle between the central and provincial governments, Ota's campaign went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled against him last August.
But a month later, Okinawan voters overwhelmingly supported Ota's stance in an unprecedented referendum calling for the removal of the U.S. bases.
